Editions
What is the main difference between Windows PowerShell 5.1 and PowerShell 7?
5.1 is built into Windows on .NET Framework; 7 is cross-platform on modern .NET
5.1 runs only on Linux servers; 7 runs only on Windows desktop editions
5.1 is a graphical tool; 7 is a command-line tool with no scripting support
5.1 is the newer release; 7 is the older edition kept for compatibility
Windows PowerShell 5.1 ships with Windows. PowerShell 7 is installed separately and runs on Windows, Linux and macOS.
m
Cmdlet naming
Which name follows PowerShell's approved Verb-Noun convention?
Get-Service
Service-Get
ListServices
svc_get
Cmdlets use an approved verb, a hyphen and a singular noun, such as Get-Service or Stop-Process.
m
Discovering commands
Which command finds cmdlets whose noun contains 'Event'?
Get-Command -Noun *Event*
Find-Event -All
Get-Help Event -List
Show-Command Event*
Get-Command searches available commands by verb, noun or name.
m
Help
Which command shows examples for Get-Process?
Get-Help Get-Process -Examples
Get-Process -Help
man Get-Process -All
Show-Examples Get-Process
Get-Help with -Examples shows usage examples; Update-Help downloads current help.
d
Objects not text
Why does Get-Process | Where-Object CPU -gt 100 work without parsing columns?
Each item is an object with a CPU property
PowerShell converts the table to CSV first
Where-Object reads the screen output text
CPU is a reserved keyword in the shell
The pipeline passes .NET objects, so filters use properties directly rather than text positions.
m
Core pipeline cmdlets
Which cmdlet chooses particular properties to keep from each object?
Select-Object
Where-Object
Sort-Object
Measure-Object
Select-Object picks properties; Where-Object filters items; Sort-Object orders them.
d
Format versus export
Why should Format-Table not appear before Export-Csv in a pipeline?
Format-Table emits formatting objects, not the original data
Export-Csv cannot write files with more than ten columns
Format-Table deletes properties that have empty values
Export-Csv requires its input to be sorted by name first
Format-* cmdlets are for display only; export the original objects instead.
d
Calculated properties
What does @{Name='MB';Expression={$_.WS/1MB}} do in a Select-Object call?
Adds a computed property showing working set in megabytes
Renames the WS property and deletes the original value
Filters out processes using less than one megabyte
Converts every property on the object to megabytes
A calculated property defines a new property name and a script block that computes its value.
m
Providers
What does a PowerShell provider such as HKLM: allow?
Browsing the registry with the same cmdlets used for files
Connecting to a remote computer without credentials
Running Linux commands natively inside PowerShell
Encrypting the registry before it is changed
Providers expose data stores (file system, registry, certificates) as drives navigable with Get-ChildItem and similar cmdlets.
m
Variables
How is a variable written in PowerShell?
With a $ prefix, as in $count
With a % prefix, as in %count%
With an @ prefix, as in @count
With no prefix, as in count
PowerShell variables start with $. %VAR% is cmd.exe syntax.
m
Operators
Which operator tests numeric equality in PowerShell?
-eq
-is
Comparison uses -eq, -ne, -gt and similar; = is assignment.
d
Hash tables
Which structure stores key-value pairs in PowerShell?
@{ Key = 'Value' }
@( 'Key', 'Value' )
[ 'Key' => 'Value' ]
{ Key: Value }
@{} creates a hash table; @() creates an array.
d
String expansion
Why is building a command string from user input and running it with Invoke-Expression unsafe?
The input can inject additional commands
Invoke-Expression ignores every variable
Invoke-Expression needs administrator rights
The string is executed only on remote hosts
Invoke-Expression runs any text as code. Pass input as parameters instead of concatenating it into commands.
m
Advanced functions
What does adding [CmdletBinding()] to a function provide?
Common parameters such as -Verbose and -ErrorAction
Automatic conversion of the function into a compiled binary
Permission to run the function without an execution policy
A graphical form for entering the function's parameters
CmdletBinding makes a function behave like a cmdlet, including common parameters.
d
Parameter validation
What does [ValidateSet('Start','Stop')] on a parameter do?
Rejects any value other than Start or Stop before the body runs
Sets Start as the default value when Stop is not supplied
Converts any value passed in to either Start or Stop automatically
Runs the function twice, once with Start and once with Stop
Validation attributes check input up front and give clear errors, a simple defensive habit.
d
Error handling
Why might a try/catch block not catch an error from Get-Item on a missing path?
Non-terminating errors are not caught unless -ErrorAction Stop is used
try/catch works only for errors from external programs, not cmdlets
Get-Item never returns an error when a path does not exist
catch blocks run only when the script is executed as administrator
Many cmdlet errors are non-terminating. -ErrorAction Stop turns them into terminating errors that catch can handle.
m
WhatIf
What does -WhatIf do on a cmdlet such as Remove-Item?
Shows what would happen without making the change
Asks for confirmation before each individual item
Runs the command and then undoes it automatically
Logs the change to the security event log only
-WhatIf previews the operation; -Confirm prompts for each change.
d
Execution policy
Why is the execution policy not a security boundary?
It is a safety feature that users can bypass, for example per process
It is enforced only on domain controllers and never on workstations
It blocks every script, including signed scripts from Microsoft
It only applies to scripts stored on network drives
Microsoft describes execution policy as preventing accidental script runs. Enforcement needs application control such as WDAC or AppLocker.
m
Script signing
What does signing a PowerShell script with a trusted certificate show?
Who published it and that it has not changed since signing
That the script contains no vulnerabilities or bugs
That the script will run faster on every system
That the script was reviewed by Microsoft before release
A signature proves origin and integrity, not that the code is safe.
d
JEA
What does Just Enough Administration (JEA) provide?
Remote endpoints that let users run only approved commands, often as a virtual account
A licence that allows administrators to install PowerShell 7 on servers
A tool that converts PowerShell scripts into Group Policy objects
A built-in antivirus engine that scans every script before it runs
JEA constrains remote sessions to specific cmdlets and parameters, implementing least privilege for administration.
m
AMSI
What does the Antimalware Scan Interface (AMSI) let security products do?
Scan script content after de-obfuscation, before it runs
Encrypt PowerShell scripts stored on the disk
Block every script that downloads data from the internet
Replace PowerShell with a safer scripting language
AMSI passes script buffers to the antimalware engine at run time, including dynamically generated code.
m
Logging features
Which PowerShell logging feature records the content of executed script blocks?
Script Block Logging
Transcription
Module Logging only
Execution policy logging
Script Block Logging (Event ID 4104) captures the code that runs, including de-obfuscated content.
d
Transcription
What does PowerShell transcription record?
The input and output of sessions to text files
Only the errors raised by failed commands
The network packets sent by PowerShell
The registry changes made during a session
Transcripts log what was typed and displayed. They complement Script Block Logging, which logs the code.
m
Reading events
Which channel holds PowerShell Script Block Logging events?
Microsoft-Windows-PowerShell/Operational
System
Application
Security
Event ID 4104 is written to the PowerShell Operational log.
d
Protecting logs
Why should PowerShell logs be forwarded off the endpoint?
An attacker with admin rights can clear local logs
Local logs are deleted every time PowerShell closes
Forwarded logs are automatically decrypted
Endpoints cannot store more than one hour of logs
Central collection preserves evidence even if the host's logs are cleared or tampered with.
d
Obfuscation
Why do defenders treat the -EncodedCommand parameter with suspicion?
It hides the command text from casual inspection and is common in attacks
It always means the script came from Microsoft's own update servers
It disables all logging, so nothing about the command can be recorded
It can only be used by the SYSTEM account during the boot process
Base64-encoded commands are legitimate but frequently abused. Script Block Logging records the decoded content.
